scenes.description: A panel discussion on the ethical implications of life science advancements is underway. Dylan Wilson, a 30-year-old life scientist and radical advocate for technological progress, is the featured speaker. He is joined by two other experts, Dr. Ting Zhao and Mr. Bobby Lang, who represent more cautious perspectives.

characters.name: Dylan Wilson
characters.description: A confident and sharp 30-year-old life science researcher, known for his radical views and determination to push boundaries in biotechnology.; years old / Male / Life Scientist, 30 years old; Occupation: Life Science Researcher; Personality: Radical, Confident, Sharp, Determined; Values: Technological breakthrough, Innovation, Challenging ideas; Interests: Biotechnology, Philosophy of science, Ethical debate; Experiences: Speaking at academic conferences, Publishing research papers, Hosting controversial topic discussions

characters.name: Dr. Ting Zhao
characters.description: A 45-year-old bioethicist with a calm and analytical demeanor, focused on the moral implications of scientific progress; Female; Age: 45; Occupation: Professor of Bioethics and Research Ethics Consultant; Personality: Thoughtful, principled, empathetic; Values: Human dignity, responsible innovation, transparency; Interests: Medical philosophy, cross-cultural ethics, literature; Experiences: Led ethics review for a controversial gene-editing trial in China, published extensively on the societal impact of biotechnology, advised international health organizations on policy frameworks.

characters.name: Mr. Bobby Lang
characters.description: A 52-year-old environmental consultant who emphasizes ecological balance and sustainability in all discussions; Male; Age: 52; Occupation: Environmental Consultant and Sustainability Advisor; Personality: Analytical, cautious, empathetic; Values: Ecological integrity, long-term responsibility, transparency; Interests: Birdwatching, environmental policy debates, organic gardening; Experiences: Worked on reforestation projects in deforested regions of Southeast Asia, advised local governments on sustainable urban development, witnessed negative impacts of unchecked biotech experiments on ecosystems.

actions.dialogue: We stand at the precipice of a new era in life science. The question is no longer whether we can extend life, but whether we should. I ask you: do we really have a 'duty to die' in a world where technology can break the natural limits of aging?
Dylan, your argument is compelling, but doesn't it ignore the ethical implications of playing god with human life? What about the potential for inequality and the sanctity of natural life cycles?
I agree with Ting. Even if we could eliminate aging, what about the strain on our planet's resources? Longer life for a few might mean fewer resources for the many.
I see your points, but I believe the duty to die is a myth. Nature is not a moral compass; it's a system we can optimize. If we can reduce suffering and increase productivity, why would we not do so?
But Dylan, isn't the value of life tied to its impermanence? What happens when we remove the urgency that shapes human ambition and empathy?
And even if we solve the ethical questions, can we guarantee that this technology won't be exploited by those in power for their own gain?
That's the price of innovation. We must not let fear paralyze progress. The duty to die is a relic of the past, and I'm here to challenge that narrative.

scenes.plot: Dylan Wilson's provocative question about the 'duty to die' ignites a heated but respectful debate with Dr. Ting Zhao and Mr. Bobby Lang. Their exchange highlights the tension between radical technological optimism and ethical caution, drawing the audience into a deeper consideration of the future of life science.
scenes.social_purpose: To showcase Dylan's personality and values through a debate, while also emphasizing the broader societal implications of his work and beliefs.
